title: Power Factor Correction: Reactive Power Mitigation & Phasor Analysis

content.aim: To demonstrate power factor correction in single-phase AC circuits by connecting shunt capacitor across inductive load, thereby reducing reactive power, minimizing supply current and improving power factor toward unity. The experiment also verifies relationships between real, reactive and apparent power and that parallel branch currents add as phasors.
objectives: To verify relationships between real power P (W), reactive power Q (VAR), apparent power S (VA) and power factor cosθ.
To verify that for pure resistance P=VI (cosθ=1), for pure reactance P≈0 (cosθ≈0), for R+L composite P<VI (0<cosθ<1), and that total line current is phasor sum not arithmetic sum of branch currents.
To measure supply current A1 and load current A2 as load switches operated across R-only, L-only, R+L and R+L+C configurations.
To construct phasor diagrams showing how leading capacitor current cancels lagging inductor current without changing real power.
To calculate capacitance required for unity power factor and confirm current minimization experimentally.

theory.text:
Power Triangle and Power Factor

For sinusoidal AC with voltage v(t)=√2 V cos(ωt) and current lagging by θ, i(t)=√2 I cos(ωt-θ), instantaneous power p(t)=v(t)i(t)=VI cosθ(1+cos2ωt)+VI sinθ sin2ωt. Averaging over cycle gives:

• Active power P = VI cosθ (W) - average rate of energy conversion to useful work, heat or light.

• Reactive power Q = VI sinθ (VAR) - amplitude of energy oscillating between source and magnetic fields of inductors or electric fields of capacitors.

Apparent power S = VI (VA) determines sizing of alternators, transformers and cables:

S = √(P²+Q²)
PF = P/S = cosθ

Shunt Capacitor Correction

Most industrial loads (induction motors, welders, transformers) are inductive and require lagging magnetizing current IL sinθ. Total current:

IL = IL cosθ - j IL sinθ = IR - j IM

Shunt capacitor draws leading current 90° ahead:

IC = +j V/XC = +j ωCV = +j 2πfCV

KCL at supply node:

Isupply = IL + IC = IL cosθ + j(2πfCV - IL sinθ)

Capacitor supplies magnetizing energy locally, circulating reactive energy between inductor and capacitor. Utility supply relieved of reactive current. Active component IR = IL cosθ remains unchanged as load power constant. In this experiment, wattmeter remained ~334W while supply current dropped from 2.55A to 1.67A.

Required Capacitance for Target Power Factor

Let initial PF be cosθ1 lagging, target cosθ2. Q1 = P tanθ1, Q2 = P tanθ2. Capacitor must supply QC = Q1-Q2 = P(tanθ1-tanθ2). Since QC = V²/XC = ωCV² =2πfCV²:

C = P(tanθ1-tanθ2)/(2πfV²)

For unity PF (cosθ2=1, θ2=0, tanθ2=0):

Cunity = P tanθ1/(2πfV²) = IL sinθ1/(2πfV)

For combined R+L load, optimum was 8.8µF as measured, giving unity PF and minimum supply current.

Benefits of Power Factor Correction

• Reduction in I²R losses: Ploss = Isupply² Rline = (P/(V cosθ))² Rline. Improving PF from 0.55 to 1.0 reduces current 45% and losses by 1-(0.55)²=69.75%.

• Avoidance of utility penalties for low PF (typically below 0.85-0.90) due to excessive kVA demand.

• Release of transformer kVA capacity, allowing load expansion without larger transformer.

• Improved voltage regulation by reducing inductive voltage drop ΔV≈IRcosθ+IXsinθ along feeders.

Over-compensation and Resonance

Over-compensation (C>Cunity) causes leading PF and voltage rise due to leading current through inductive line reactance: ΔV≈Ilead*Xline with opposite sign to lagging drop, causing secondary voltage to exceed nominal. Shunt capacitors can form resonance with system inductance at harmonic frequencies. Resonance frequency fres = f1 * √(Ssc/QC), where Ssc is short-circuit kVA. If fres coincides with harmonic from non-linear loads (5th=250Hz, 7th=350Hz, 11th=550Hz), large harmonic currents cause capacitor overload and fuse blowing. Detuned reactors (e.g., 7% reactor) added in series with capacitors to shift resonance below harmonic frequencies. This is relevant in Nigerian distribution networks with many non-linear loads.

Additional Analysis: Phasor Diagram Construction and Power Calculations

Phasor diagrams were constructed to scale using measured voltages and currents. For uncompensated R+L load, total current is vector sum of resistive branch current IR in phase with V and inductive branch current IL lagging V by θL. IR = V/R = 200V/145Ω =1.38A, IL = V/ZL, where ZL = √(rL²+XL²). From Test 2, ZL=111.11Ω, rL=18Ω, XL=109.64Ω, so IL=1.80A lagging by θL=arccos(rL/ZL)=80.68°. Total current Itotal = IR + IL cosθL - j IL sinθL =1.38+1.80*0.162 - j1.80*0.9868=1.67-j1.77A, magnitude 2.43A, close to measured 2.55A. Real power P = V*IR + V*IL cosθL =200*1.38+200*0.29=276+58=334W, matching wattmeter 334.3W. Reactive power Q = V*IL sinθL =200*1.77=354VAR lagging.

When capacitor C=8.8µF added, capacitive current IC=ωCV=2π*50*8.8e-6*200=1.77A leading 90°. Total current becomes Isupply = (IR+IL cosθL) + j(IC - IL sinθL) =1.67 + j(1.77-1.77)=1.67A in phase with V, giving unity PF. Real power unchanged P=334W, reactive power Q≈0, apparent power S=334VA, PF=1.0. Supply current minimized from 2.55A to 1.67A, reduction 34.5%, while load current through R+L remains 2.55A.

If C increased to 16µF, IC=2π*50*16e-6*200=3.02A leading, net reactive current =3.02-1.77=1.25A leading, total current Isupply=√(1.67²+1.25²)=2.09A (measured 2.18A), PF leading 0.769, showing over-compensation increases current again and causes voltage rise.

Economic and Technical Benefits

Power factor correction reduces line current for same real power, reducing I²R losses in cables and transformers. For example, improving PF from 0.655 to 1.0 reduces current from 2.55A to 1.67A, losses proportional to I² reduce by factor (1.67/2.55)²=0.428, i.e., 57.2% reduction in losses. For industrial loads of hundreds of kW, this is significant energy saving and reduced heating, extending equipment life.

Utility companies charge penalty for low PF because low PF requires larger kVA capacity for same kW, increasing investment in generation, transmission and distribution. In Nigeria, many industrial customers are penalized if PF below 0.85-0.90. Installing capacitor banks near loads improves PF, avoids penalty and frees transformer capacity for additional loads without upgrading transformer.

Voltage regulation also improves with PF correction because inductive voltage drop I*X sinθ along line is reduced. For lagging PF, voltage drop ΔV≈IRcosθ+IXsinθ. Reducing sinθ component reduces drop, improving voltage at load terminals. Over-compensation with leading PF can cause voltage rise ΔV≈-IC Xline, potentially exceeding nominal voltage and stressing equipment, so optimum PF is typically 0.95-1.0 lagging, not leading.

Harmonic resonance is concern with capacitor banks in presence of non-linear loads generating harmonics (5th,7th,11th from VFDs, rectifiers). Shunt capacitor forms parallel resonant circuit with system inductance at fres = f1 * √(Ssc/QC). If fres coincides with harmonic frequency, large harmonic currents circulate, overloading capacitor and causing fuse blowing or capacitor failure. Detuned reactors (e.g., 7% reactor, i.e., XL=0.07 XC at fundamental) added in series with capacitor shift resonance below 5th harmonic, avoiding resonance. Modern PFC systems use detuned or tuned filters to mitigate harmonics.

procedure: Circuit assembled as per Figure 3. Knife switches S1,S2,S3 placed in open position. Auto-transformer (Variac) connected to AC mains with dial at zero volts before switching ON. Wiring, meter ratings and ground connections inspected before energizing.
AC mains switched ON, Variac gradually increased until voltmeter V read exactly 200.0V RMS. This voltage maintained constant throughout tests to keep calculations consistent.
Resistive load (R only): Switch S1 closed, S2,S3 open. Supply ammeter A1, load ammeter A2, voltmeter V and wattmeter P recorded. A1=A2 and cosθ≈1.0 verified, with P=VI=276W.

Inductive load (L only): S1 opened, S2 closed, S3 open. Meters A1,A2,V,P recorded. Real power small (58.3W copper winding loss I²rL), apparent power 360VA, low lagging PF 0.162 confirming pure inductance consumes negligible net power.

Combined uncompensated R+L: Both S1 and S2 closed, S3 open. All meters recorded. Total current A1=2.55A noted to be less than arithmetic sum 1.38+1.80=3.18A, confirming vector addition. Uncompensated PF≈0.655 lag calculated.

Power factor correction sweep (R+L+C): Capacitor switch S3 closed. Decade capacitance box increased from 2.5µF to 16.0µF as in Table 305.1. At each step, load current A2 remained constant at 2.55A and wattmeter P constant at ~334W, while supply current A1 decreased from 2.55A to minimum 1.67A at C=8.8µF (unity PF) then increased with leading PF. Apparent power S, cosθ and Q calculated for each setting and plotted as Graph 305.1.
After tests, Variac set to zero, AC mains switched OFF, S3 opened and capacitor box discharged through safety probe before dismantling to avoid residual charge hazard.
precautions: AC capacitors retain peak charge Vpeak=√2*200V≈283V after disconnection. Discharge resistors checked and capacitor terminals shorted with insulated probe before handling to avoid electric shock.

Inductive current not interrupted abruptly while high current flowed through inductor to avoid flyback voltage v=L di/dt that can cause shock and damage meters. Variac de-energized before altering connections.

Wattmeter current coil connected in series and potential coil in parallel. Voltage rating 250V and current rating 5.0A not exceeded. Wattmeter can burn from overcurrent even with low deflection at poor power factor.
Ammeter and wattmeter scale multiplication factors verified to avoid transcription errors, as laboratory meters have multipliers.
content.discussion:
Measurements in Table 305.1 validate four theoretical statements:

(a) Pure resistance (Test 1): P=276.0W, VI=200.0*1.38=276.0VA, P=VI, cosθ=1.000, confirming active power equals volt-amperes for resistive load.

(b) Pure inductance (Test 2): Apparent power S=360.0VA, wattmeter 58.3W. Residual power is copper loss in coil winding resistance rL = P/I² =58.3/3.24=18.0Ω. Reactive component Q=√(360²-58.3²)=355.2VAR, showing ideal reactor consumes zero net power, with small real loss due to winding resistance.

(c) R+L (Test 3): P=334.3W, S=510.0VA, P<VI, cosθ=0.655 lagging, confirming composite load has P<VI.

(d) Vector addition: Total current A1=2.55A is less than arithmetic sum IR+IL=1.38+1.80=3.18A. Vector calculation: Itotal=(IR+ILcosθL)-j(ILsinθL)=1.67-j1.77A, magnitude √(1.67²+1.77²)=2.43A, close to measured 2.55A (4.9% error due to tolerance and meter accuracy), confirming phasor addition must be used for AC branch currents.

Current Reduction and Resonance Curve

As capacitance increased from 2.5µF to 16µF:

• Capacitive leading current IC=ωCV increased and cancelled lagging magnetizing current IM=1.77A. At C=8.8µF, IC=2π*50*8.8e-6*200=1.77A, exactly cancelling IM. Supply current reached minimum IR=1.67A, PF=1.000, as shown in Graph 305.1.

• During sweep, load current A2 stayed constant at 2.55A and real power P constant at ~334.9W. Load received same voltage and did same work, but supply current dropped by 34.5%, demonstrating industrial value: same real work with less line current, lower I²R losses and reduced kVA demand.

• Beyond 8.8µF (e.g., 16µF), circuit became over-compensated: leading current exceeded lagging, PF=0.769 leading and supply current rose to 2.18A. Hence optimum capacitance exists; more capacitance is not always better and can cause voltage rise.

Graph of supply current versus capacitance shows V-shaped curve with minimum at unity PF, while PF versus capacitance rises from 0.655 lag to 1.0 then goes leading. Wattmeter reading remaining constant confirms capacitor supplies only reactive power, not real power, so kWh consumption unchanged but kVA demand reduced.

The experiment demonstrates why industrial capacitor banks are installed near inductive loads to improve power factor, reduce losses, avoid utility penalties and free transformer capacity. Over-compensation and harmonic resonance must be considered in design, requiring detuned reactors in presence of non-linear loads.

content.conclusion:
Experiment verified statements (a)-(d): P=VI for pure R, P≈0 for pure L (except winding resistance), P<VI for R+L, and parallel AC currents add as phasors not arithmetically (2.55A ≠ 3.18A). Shunt capacitor supplied lagging reactive current locally, improving PF from 0.655 lagging to 1.000 unity at Copt=8.8µF. Supply current reduced from 2.55A to 1.67A (34.5% reduction) while real power remained ~334.9W, demonstrating value of power factor correction in reducing transmission losses and freeing system capacity. Over-compensation beyond optimum caused leading PF and increase in supply current, showing need to design for optimum capacitance.

questions.question: Check the truth of statements (a) to (d) in the theory using the appropriate numerical figures recorded in your experimental table.
questions.answer:
(a) Pure R Test 1: V=200V, I=1.38A, P=276W, VI=276VA, P=VI, cosθ=1.000 TRUE.
(b) Pure L Test 2: S=360VA, P=58.3W, which equals I²rL=1.8²*18=58.3W from winding resistance, pure reactance consumes 0W TRUE.
(c) R+L Test 3: P=334.3W, VI=510VA, P<VI, cosθ=0.655 TRUE.
(d) Vector sum Test 3: IR=1.38A, IL=1.80A, arithmetic sum 3.18A, measured total 2.55A, 2.55≠3.18, proving phasor sum TRUE. All statements verified.

questions.question: Calculate the exact power factor of the following loads: (a) \(L\) only, (b) \(L\) and \(R\) only.
questions.answer:
(a) L only: S=200*1.80=360VA, P=58.3W, PF=P/S=58.3/360=0.162 lagging, θL=80.68°.
(b) L+R: S=200*2.55=510VA, P=334.3W, PF=334.3/510=0.655 lagging, θ=49.08°. After adding 8.8µF capacitor, PF became 1.0 unity.

questions.question: From the value of \(I\) and the calculated power factor for \(L\) only, calculate \(\sin\theta\). Compare with the value of \(\mathit{I}_{C}\) and construct the values obtained for \(L\) and \(C\) in the circuit.
questions.answer: L only: IL=1.80A, cosθL=0.162, sinθL=√(1-0.162²)=0.9868. Reactive component IM=IL sinθL=1.776A. For correction, IC=IM=1.776A. XC=V/IC=200/1.776=112.61Ω, C=1/(2πfXC)=28.26µF for L alone. Impedance ZL=V/IL=111.11Ω, rL=ZL cosθL=18Ω, XL=ZL sinθL=109.64Ω, L=XL/(2πf)=0.349H≈0.35H. For combined R+L load, optimum was 8.8µF as measured.

questions.question: Check by calculation the value of supply current taken when \(R\) and \(C\) are in circuit (with \(L\) disconnected) and compare with the measured value.
questions.answer: R-C with C=8.8µF: IR=1.38A in phase, IC=2πfCV=2π*50*8.8e-6*200=0.553A leading 90°. Isupply=√(IR²+IC²)=√(1.38²+0.553²)=1.487A. Measured A1=1.49A, error 0.20%, confirming quadrature phasor addition.

questions.question: Explain the catastrophic dangers of "Over-Compensation" and Series/Parallel Harmonic Resonance in industrial power factor correction installations.
questions.answer: Over-compensation (C>Cunity) causes leading PF and voltage rise: ΔV = j Ilead Xline = -IC Xline, secondary voltage rises above nominal, stressing insulation. Harmonic resonance: Non-linear loads (VFDs, rectifiers) inject harmonics (5th,7th,11th). Shunt capacitor forms parallel resonant circuit with transformer leakage inductance at fres = f1 * √(Ssc/QC). If fres coincides with harmonic (e.g., 250Hz for 5th), impedance rises sharply, large harmonic currents cause capacitor rupture, transformer heating and fuse blowing. Modern PFC banks include detuning reactors (e.g., 7% reactor) in series with capacitors to shift resonance below harmonic frequencies.

learnings: Experimental proof that AC branch currents add as phasors, not arithmetically, requiring resolution into active and reactive components for correct analysis.
How shunt capacitors act as local reactive power sources, supplying magnetizing current at load terminals and reducing burden on utility lines, principle used in industrial capacitor banks.

Observation of V-shaped curve of line current versus capacitance with minimum at unity power factor, and that wattmeter measures only active power while apparent power must be checked for instrument protection.
Understanding of over-compensation and harmonic resonance risks in industrial PFC installations and need for detuned reactors in presence of non-linear loads.
